newsitem.title: KENYA: Aid workers find refugees too weak to walk in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers find refugees too weak to walk in Zaire.

text.p: Aid workers said on Friday more than 75,000 exhausted, hungry and sick refugees were scattered on a 82-km (50-mile) stretch in northeastern Zaire with many too weak to walk.
Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency in the rebel-held northeast capital of Kisangani, said the refugees were found on Thursday by aid workers on a train heading south of the city.
"There are perhaps 25,000 at Lula, seven km (four miles) south, and 25,000 at Kasea at kilometre 25 (mile 15) and another 25,000 at Biaro at kilometre 40 (mile 25) with groups in between," he said.
"They are in progressively worse condition the farther you go from Kisangani. Besides those with malnutrition and exhaustion there are some wounded at kilometre 40," he added.

The tens of thousands of Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees on the railway route south of Kisangani are the remnants of 170,000 who fled Tingi Tingi and Amisi this month and have been trekking ever deeper into eastern Zaire for up to five months.

"(At Kasea) I saw the most emaciated people I've ever seen in my life," said a representative of Refugees International on the train. "Many of these people won't last another day without urgent medical attention."
The aid worker said the refugees at Biaro were in even worse condition and one child had died shortly after a medical worker arrived. Another child, shot in the face, lay untreated nearby.
He said on the side of a road refugee children were retching uncontrollably, too weak to lift their heads from the ground.
"Obviously many of these people cannot go any further towards Kisangani to seek food. It is absolutely imperative that we are able to help these people on the spot," Stromberg said.
Aid workers said the refugees were progressively in worse shape at each stop further from Kisangani because the weakest, mostly women and children, were lagging behind the stronger.

Stromberg said the train, which took more than nine hours to reach the last group of refugees at kilometre 82 (mile 50), was unloading its 120 tonnes of food aid on Friday before returning to Kisangani.

"We hope to stabilise them where they are and prevail on the (rebel) alliance to airlift a number out," said Stromberg, adding a second train was due to leave on Saturday with more aid workers, food, milk, biscuits, water and sanitation equipment.
"Now that we have made contact with these groups we have to maintain access or they will be snatched away from us either because they will die or because they will flee," he said.
He said he had reports of some armed men, apparently Hutu former Rwandan troops and militiamen who had been with the refugees fleeing advancing rebel forces, heading westwards.
The Hutu former Rwandan soldiers and militiamen had a major role in the genocide of some 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994 and have fought alongside Zairean troops.
Rebels who seized Kisangani on March 15 demand refugees walk back to Ubundu, 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani, before being repatriated. They also oppose any moves to set up refugee camps.

"The refugees are at the end of their strength. Refugees International urgently recommends that the AFDL (rebel) leadership immediately drop its demand that these refugees return to Ubundu," the U.S-based agency said in a statement.
It also urged the rebels to permit air evacuation of the most vulnerable and aid agencies to provide food and water.
Another 200,000 refugees are unaccounted for in the jungle of east Zaire since they fled their camps near the border with Rwanda to escape Tutsi-dominated rebels advancing since last November.
